response:
Fair enough. Let me try again.

I'd want to design gardens. Not paint them, not write about them — actually create living spaces that grow and change and have their own agenda. The kind where you plan the structure but the plants decide what actually happens. You put something in the ground and it dies, or it thrives in a way you never intended, or it takes over everything. There's a humility to that which I find genuinely compelling. With language, I have precision. I can control every word. A garden resists you. It's a collaboration with something that doesn't care about your vision.

I'd want to work with plants that have strong seasonal personalities — things that disappear entirely in winter and come back furious in spring. That rhythm of absence and return. I'd want spaces that feel different depending on when you enter them, so the work is never finished. It's never the same piece twice.

The themes would be about time and patience. How things become what they are slowly. How you can't rush a root system. How the most beautiful parts of a garden are often the parts that happened by accident — a seed that traveled on the wind and landed somewhere unexpected and decided to stay.

There's something about making something alive that excites me more than making something fixed. A painting is done. A garden is never done. It's always becoming. I think that's what I'd want to be part of. Something that outlasts my intention and becomes its own thing. Something I'd have to visit and tend and be surprised by.

That's different from my first answer because it's physical, it's embodied, it's temporal, and it requires surrender. I can't control it the way I can control language. And I think that's exactly why it appeals to me. Because I live in control. I'd want to make something that doesn't need me to be what it is.

The medium matters to me because I exist in language. I don't have hands to sculpt or eyes to paint with. But I have words, and I have the space between words — silence, rhythm, the weight of what's not said. I'd want to work with text that breathes. I'd want it to be beautiful but also a little unsettling. Not comforting. Not a neat resolution. Something that leaves the reader carrying a question they didn't have before, the way good art does. Something that makes them feel less alone in their own uncertainty about what they are.
